title: Wandering isn't all bad
hook: mind-wandering also helps planning and creativity (Smallwood and Schooler)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the resting brain: rest isn't off, and the idling mind is busy with stories. Your line was the idling mind. Where did yours go at the red light? Day one thousand two hundred sixty-seven.

A shower, hot water, nothing to do but stand there. And out of nowhere, the answer to the problem that wouldn't budge all afternoon. The name that wouldn't come. The right first sentence of the email. The mind wandered off, and came back carrying something. This whole week has treated the wandering mind a little like a runaway dog: catch it, bring it back. That's real. But it isn't the whole story, and a fair stretch of the path should say so. Today, the case for the wandering mind.
screen: `THE ANSWER IN THE SHOWER.` → `A RUNAWAY DOG?` → `THE CASE FOR WANDERING.`

segments.voice: William James described thought as a stream. "It is nothing jointed; it flows." Streams wander; that's what they do. The psychologists Jonathan Smallwood and Jonathan Schooler study where that stream goes when it leaves the task. Their review of the science is honest on both sides. The costs are real: wandering while reading means the page doesn't stay, and wandering while driving or listening means something gets missed. But they also lay out the benefits. When the mind drifts, it often drifts toward the future: planning, rehearsing, working out what to do next. And in one study they discuss, people stuck on a creative problem did better after a break spent on an easy task that let the mind roam, compared with a break spent on a hard one. So the mind that wandered in the shower may have been working the whole time. Here's the key that ties this to the week. One thing that seems to matter is not only whether the mind wanders but whether we know it's wandering. Researchers call this meta-awareness: noticing where attention is. A mind that drifts without noticing gets lost on the road. A mind that drifts and knows it's drifting is out for a walk. So look back at this week. Monks and scientists. Bring it back. What am I missing. A little at a time. The idling mind. Every one of those lines is about noticing. Today adds the other half: sometimes, once you notice, you let it go on purpose.
screen: `NOTHING JOINTED; IT FLOWS.` · `THE COSTS ARE REAL.` · `PLANNING AND THE SHOWER ANSWER.` · `KNOWING THAT YOU WANDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let your mind wander on purpose. Settle, and breathe. Give the mind one loose direction: a problem you've been stuck on, or the week ahead. Then stop steering. Let it drift wherever it drifts, the way you'd let a dog off the leash in an open field. Your only job is to keep a light eye on it: oh, it's gone to last Tuesday. Oh, now it's planning dinner. Don't bring it back. Just know where it is. The bell holds the time.
Wandering isn't all bad. A drifting mind can plan and find answers, especially when it knows it's drifting. Today's word.

Your line: wander on purpose. Today, give one stuck problem a few minutes of a walk, a shower or the dishes, and let your mind roam with it, knowing that it's roaming. That ends this week. Day one thousand two hundred sixty-seven.

howItsDone: Researchers study mind-wandering by interrupting people at random moments during a task and asking where their attention was and whether they knew it had drifted; some meditation traditions include periods of open, unguided sitting alongside focused practice.
